k: Getting a legal document sent right, the first time

Banks, insurers and financial companies use the platform to stamp and send documents for signing, at high volume and under strict compliance. The old flow put everything on one crowded screen and quietly chose for people. I led the redesign into a clear, guided flow. It’s now live with customers.
Another designer, a product manager, 4 developers
A crowded screen, with legal consequences

For banking, financial services and insurance clients, a document sent with the wrong stamp duty, signer or setting isn’t a small mistake. It can mean a rejected document, a delayed customer and a compliance problem.
The old flow made those mistakes easy. Four problems stood out.
“Upload” was always pre-selected, so many people never noticed they could start from a template.
One dense screen showed every field, setting and the document preview together.
People couldn’t tell what they’d finished or what was left, so they felt they were skipping something.
Errors caused by the unclear interface turned into frequent support requests.
I combined interviews, testing on the old flow, and a close look at how others solve the same problem.
With operations managers, product admins and compliance officers, across different roles and teams.
People used the old flow while describing what they were doing and thinking.
Post-session surveys, feedback from sales, support and demos, an audit of the old flow, and a study of DocuSign, Adobe Acrobat Sign, Leegality and Digio.
“I didn’t even know Template was an option because Upload was always pre-selected.”
“I felt like I was skipping something. It was hard to track what I’d completed.”
“I only need the document when placing signatures. Otherwise it’s just visual noise.”
Confusing labels, and no way to go back a step
Couldn’t see all the ways to start a document
Ease of use, reuse and transparency
Too much on screen, and no clear record of what was set

I was the lead designer, working with one other designer, a product manager and four developers. I led the research, information architecture, interaction design and visual design, and worked with engineering so the new flow matched how the system actually processes a document.
One crowded screen, into seven clear steps
I broke the send into the order people actually think about it, and tested the structure with card sorting and tree testing. The structure’s score went from 60% to 85%.
Always shows where you are, what’s done and what’s left, and lets you go back.
Only the fields for the current step, nothing else.
Settings and guidance for the step, so the middle stays clear.
Principles I designed by: a light cognitive load, clear visual hierarchy, consistent patterns, components that adapt to new cases, and a polished look that builds trust.
Five decisions, and what they cost
Each change answered something people told us or did in testing.
“Upload” was always pre-selected, so people didn’t know they could start from a template.
Two clear, equal options to start: upload a document, or start from a template.
One extra click for people who always upload, in exchange for everyone seeing both paths.

k.i: Start: Upload or Template, side by side
The stepper with progress, and one step in focus

k: Seven steps instead of one screen
Showing everything at once overwhelmed people, and they couldn’t tell what was left.
A guided flow with a stepper that shows progress and lets people go back to any step.
More screens to move through, but each one is light and people always know where they are.
Show the document only when it’s needed
People only needed the document when placing signatures; the rest of the time it was noise.
The preview appears in the signature step, where people drag signers and signature boxes onto the document.
Less context in earlier steps, which is exactly what made them clearer.

k.i: Placing signature boxes on the document
The stamping step with state, article and amount

k: Choosing the state, article and amount for stamp duty was confusing, and mistakes were costly.
Clearer form fields and labels for each part of stamp duty, in a step of its own.
Still a manual choice; making it automatic was left for later.
Nothing let people check their work before a legal document went out.
A final summary of everything set, so people can verify and fix before publishing.
One more step, in exchange for catching mistakes before they reach a signer.
Tested twice, built to be used by everyone
Each version was tested with people before it moved forward.
Did people move through the steps confidently, and could they go back without losing work?
Could people place signers and signature boxes easily, with the preview only where it helped?
Colour contrast and readability to WCAG AA, full keyboard navigation and screen reader support.
The redesign is live with customers. Task success and usability scores come from usability tests on the old flow and then the new one.
People got through the flow faster, with no hunting for the next thing to do.
Clearer fields and a final summary caught mistakes before sending.
Customers and the sales team responded well to the new flow.
“I finally feel in control when setting up workflows. It just flows now.”
Volume is the reality for banking and insurance customers. The next improvements would remove the manual work that’s left.
Pick the state and document type, and the right article and amount are suggested, instead of chosen by hand.
Start from the signers, stamp and settings used last time for the same kind of document.
Send the same document to many signers at once, for high-volume processes.
Simplifying a complex process is what makes people adopt it, and guiding them one step at a time reduces errors and builds confidence.
Aligning the design with how the backend processes a document kept the flow simple for people and dependable to build.
